LESSON 64 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

Cross-Site Scripting and Output Encoding

Why untrusted data becomes active content in a browser, why encoding belongs at output and to one context at a time, and how sanitisation and safe sinks contain what encoding alone cannot.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

Cross-site scripting is when attacker-controlled content is treated as script by the browser. It is ranked highly because the script runs with the logged-in user authority, so the attacker never needs a password.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Tracing how untrusted strings reach browser rendering sinks and how context-aware encoding neutralizes execution.

01 User Content
Safe text node
02 Template Renderer
Allowed
03 Browser DOM
  1. Source: User submits profile text, search query, or URL fragment.
  2. Boundary: Application places the value into a template or DOM text property.
  3. Sink: Browser renders readable text without creating new script elements.
01 Markup / Event Payload
Unencoded sink
02 Raw HTML Sink
Unblocked
03 Script Execution
  1. Source: Attacker supplies HTML tags, event attributes, or a javascript: URL.
  2. Boundary: Value is written raw via innerHTML or unescaped template interpolation.
  3. Sink: Browser parser executes injected script inside the victim's origin and session.
01 Untrusted Input
Encoded + restricted
02 Context Encoder + CSP
Verified
03 Inert DOM Text
  1. Source: Untrusted input arrives from the request, storage, or URL.
  2. Boundary: Output is encoded for the exact context (textContent / safe HTML sanitizer) and guarded by CSP.
  3. Sink: Browser displays literal characters; inline script execution is blocked.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The flaw is a missing decision about what kind of content a value is at the point it is written into the page.
  • Encoded correctly, a value is text. Encoded wrongly or not at all, the same value can be markup or script.
  • Reflected scripting delivers the payload in the request, stored scripting saves it on the server, and DOM scripting finds it in client-side code.
  • Stored scripting is the most damaging because it reaches every visitor and needs no lure.
  • A cookie scoped to the site is a strong payload: a script that steals it gets the victim authenticated session.

The background

  • Cross-site scripting was one of the earliest named web vulnerabilities and has been a standard top finding ever since.
  • Modern templating engines introduced auto-escaping, which removed most reflected flaws for teams that used them consistently.
  • Single-page applications moved rendering into the browser, so flaws moved from the server into client-side code.
  • Content Security Policy and cookie flags were added as a second layer because encoding alone cannot catch every context.

Real-world examples

  • A search page that echoes the query without encoding lets an attacker send a link that steals a session when clicked.
  • A comment stored and later rendered on every page turns one user post into a compromise of every reader.
  • Client-side code that writes a value into the page with innerHTML reintroduces the flaw despite a safe backend.

What to look for

  • Check whether output is encoded for the specific context it lands in: HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript or CSS are different.
  • Check client-side code for direct writes of untrusted values into the page.
  • Check whether the session cookie is readable by scripts, which decides how bad a single flaw becomes.
  • Check whether a content security policy exists and is actually enforced rather than only reported.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Encode output for its context, and prefer frameworks that do this by default and only switch off when you must.
  • Keep session cookies HttpOnly so a script cannot read them even if one gets through.
  • Deploy a content security policy without unsafe-inline, so injected script is not allowed to run.
  • Use templating rather than building markup by concatenation, and sanitise where HTML is genuinely required.
  • Treat content security policy violations as reports to fix, not noise to ignore.
